Fundaments Lab: Choked Flow

Name: (leader)      Group Number:    Section Number: 
Other team members: 
(Circle the name of the person who acted as leader/coordinator this week--make sure you get a turn every 4th lab)

Spiritual Safety: This lab highlights the dynamics of compressed gases and the concept of choked flow, where the system reaches a limit determined by physical laws. In our spiritual lives, we sometimes encounter limits or constraints, such as challenges, trials, or unanswered prayers. As the late Elder Holland so passionately stated, we must keep trying and not give up. Write a sentence or two about the importance of continuing to try.

Most things that are worth it are challenging, especially at the beginning, and so it’s important to keep trying and not give up right away. It’s also important to try again after failing, because it’s pretty uncommon to accomplish something the first time without failing.

Physical Safety: Choked Flow and Tank Blowdown Labs deal with compressed air. Compressed gases, when compared to incompressible liquids, have additional safety concerns because a lot of energy can be stored in a compressed gas. If that energy is released suddenly, it can propel dust and other solids at high speed and create harmfully large sound levels. Do not place your face or head in the path of high-speed gas flow. Long pants, closed toed shoes and safety glasses must be worn at all times.

You will fill a tank with compressed air at pressure around 75 psig. The tank is rated to handle a pressure considerably larger than this. In addition, there is a pressure relief valve on the tank to release pressure if it were to get too high. Therefore, the risk of a tank rupture is negligible.


Begin your lab by holding a team planning session (3 minutes):

1.	This lab will require additional preparation time. You should have previously read the first 4 ½ pages of “Tank Blowdown Math” posted on Learning Suite, seeking to understand the principles of compressible flow and the key equations you will need to analyze your data.
2.	Review the safety information above.
3.	Make a plan for how you will complete the lab activities. Each person should fill out their own lab report as activities are completed. At the end of the hour, after shutting down equipment appropriately, get the TA to initial the end of your report.

Background: Compressible fluid mechanics governs situations in which fluid density can significantly change, either while the fluid is stored in a tank or while it is moving along a flow path. For storage of fluids, one can use an equation of state to determine density under the prevailing pressure and temperature. For flowing systems, the key principle to determine if pressure drop is enough to generate density changes is whether the fluid velocity is close to or exceeds the speed of sound. For reference, the speed of sound in air is around 340 m/s and in liquid water is around 1500 m/s.
	
The first 4 ½ pages of the document “Tank Blowdown Math” posted on Learning Suite provide needed equations and background. The document discusses the principle of choked flow which governs flow of gases through constrictions with high pressure drops.

Project: In this lab you will do a transient mass balance on a tank while filling it with compressed air. You will learn to use a gas mass flow meter. You will also determine the discharge coefficient 𝐶𝑑 for one of the orifices that can be used to empty the tank. You will need this information for Lab 11 (Tank Blowdown).

1.	Pre-Lab Preparation: Answer the following questions to prepare for the data collection and analysis
a.	What is meant by “choked flow”?
Choked flow is when the fluid is moving at the speed of sound, because it can’t move any faster then that due to a pressure differential.

b.	You are discharging an air-filled tank through a small orifice. What is the tank gauge pressure (in psig) at which the discharge will transition from choked flow to subsonic flow? Use the standard atmospheric pressure in Provo, 0.84 atm = 12.3 psi.

 
(12.3 psi)*((1.4+1)/2)^(1.4/(1.4-1))

23.28 psi


c.	The tank pressure gauge gives gauge pressure, while required thermodynamic calculations need absolute pressure. How do you convert between one and the other?
Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmosphere pressure

d.	Do an online search for "thermal mass flow meter principle of operation." Explain what you learned about how the device measures mass flow of a gas.

The device measures gas flow using two sensors. One is placed behind the other and records the temperature. It’s hotter and so it transfers heat to the gas flowing by, and then the second sensor measures the temperature of the gas after passing by the first sensor and is hotter, and then the second sensor measures the new temperature of the gas and uses the difference to calculate the heat transfer from the first sensor and then uses that to calculate the amount of gas flowing by.









e.	The mass flow meter we use in this lab gives flow in standard liters per minute (SLM). How do you convert between this quantity and a mass flow rate in units of  gram/min?
Use the standard temperature and pressure and pv = nrT to convert it to what it is in terms of the actual pressure and temperature.


2.	Familiarization. Identify the following items on the apparatus (check mark each):
a.	 x The black/red flow control knob on the building compressed air supply. Make sure it is fully open when you begin and fully closed when you are done. If the knob doesn’t turn easily it may be locked, pull the red disk out.
b.	 	x The mass flow meter on the supply line. Make sure it is plugged in and has warmed up, reading close to zero.
c.	 x The small black/red flow control knob between the mass flow meter and the tank.
d.	 x	 The pressure gauge on the tank. Turn it on.
e.	 x	 The four outlet orifices on the tank, each controlled with an on-off ball valve. The product number on each orifice gives the size: H-40BR means diameter 0.040 inch,
H-20BR means diameter 0.020 inch, etc.
f.	 x	 The two pressure relief valves with pull rings, one of which has an on-off valve.
g.	_x__ The data collection unit (ESP32) that you can connect with a Windows machine or with an android phone.


Note, that although not required, you can also collect a digital record of the temperature inside the tank, pressure, and flow rate into the tank by connecting to the ESP32 per the video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1EWYuzzjLOw 
 
3.	Fill the Tank at a fixed mass flow rate and use this to estimate actual tank volume.
a.	Start the tank empty (gauge pressure zero)
b.	Open the flow control valve and quickly adjust it to get as close to 20 SLM flow rate. Begin a stopwatch at the same time. Continue to adjust the knob to maintain 20 SLM. Record the time when this is no longer possible and flow has dropped to less than 10 SLM. Close the valve and record the tank pressure as well.

Filling time: 159 sec

Final tank gauge pressure: 68.29 psi gauge

Estimate of final tank absolute temperature: 26.73 deg C, 299.88 K

c.	Estimate the tank actual volume in liters by using a mass balance and the above data. You need to understand what exactly the flow meter is measuring. The calculation requires a single line of math once you understand the concepts. Show that your volume estimate is reasonable based on the approximate length and diameter of the tank.

20 SLM, for 159 sec
*1 min/60 sec
=53 standard liters
PV = nRT
(1 atm)(53 liters) = n * (0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K)) * (273.15 deg K)
n = 2.3645 moles


PV = nRT
(12.3 psi + 68.29 psi)

(5.4838242 atm) * V = nRT
T = 299.88 deg K
R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K)
n = 2.3645 moles

(5.4838242 atm) * V = 2.3645 moles *0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) * 299.88 deg K
= 10.6105 liters

10.61 liters (calculated value based on flow)

15 inches length
8 inches diameter
Volume = 0.012356 meters cubed
= 12.356 liters (based on estimated volume)








d.		During the filling process, you had to keep adjusting the control knob to maintain a steady flow rate. Which way did you have to adjust the knob (more open or more closed)? Explain physically why this was necessary.
More open

This was necessary because as the tank filled the pressure differential lowered and so gas entered at a lower rate and so choked flow no longer applied and we had to open the  entrance bigger to maintain the same flow rate in. 
e.	Once you conclude the filling process and the control valve is fully closed, the pressure in the tank continues to drift slightly. Why is this? (the answer is not that the gauge is wrong).
When you fill a tank and compress it you increase its internal energy and so that results in the temperature increasing. Then after you stop filling the tank the heat in the gas is transferred to the surroundings until it reaches the same temperature as room temp and so it contracts a bit and the pressure lowers a bit, resulting in the fluctuations that are observed.


4.	Determine the Discharge Coefficient for at least one orifice under choked flow conditions.
a.	To determine 𝐶𝑑 for an orifice, you need to determine the mass flow through the orifice for a given upstream tank pressure (see “Tank Blowdown Math” Eq. 12). This is best done by setting up a steady-state condition in which you are filling and emptying the tank at the same rate, so that the flow meter on the tank inlet is telling you what is going through the orifice. This should be done while maintaining the tank at high pressure and the orifice at high flowrate so that choked flow prevails and the digital measurements are more accurate.

b.	If you assume your experiment is at steady state, but it actually isn’t, your results will be inaccurate. How will you know if you have achieved steady-state conditions in your experiment? In other words, what physical evidence will you use to determine this? Be specific.

Pressure stays the same while mass flow rate remains constant.




c.	Record below the results for at least one experiment and at least one orifice.


32.2 standard liters per minute at a pressure of 41.1 psi gauge
H-40BR label
0.040 inch diameter  0.00125663706 inches squared  area in meters squared: 8.10733588e-7


d.	When done with the experiment, leave the tank depressurized with all valves closed.

e.	How long did it take to achieve steady-state behavior in your experiment? Can anything be done to decrease this time?

It took us 2 minutes. That was partly due to not knowing what flow rate we were targeting and needing to fiddle with the controls to find the proper flow rate. If we had already calculated the flow rate beforehand, we would have known exactly what we were targeting and we would have been able to get there quicker. 

Determine 𝐶𝑑 for at least one orifice from your results in part b. Show your calculations. Is your result reasonable? Explain.

 
 

32.2 standard liters per minute = 0.00053666666 cubic standard meters per second

area in meters squared: 8.10733588 * 10^-7

12.3 psi + 41.1 psi = absolute = 51.4 psi
Converted to atm = 3.633654 atm (P_tank)

299.88 deg K (T_tank)

Cstd = 340 m/s
Pstd = 1 atm
Tstd = 273.15 deg K

y = 1.4

(I plugged all the above values into equation 12 above and solved)

= 0.9701308

Cd = 0.9701308
Is my answer reasonable? Well, it’s between 0.6 and 0.98, so that’s a good first sign. Now it just depends on if the nozzle is smoothly tapering or sharp edged. The nozzle we did the measurement for looked smoothly tapered and so yes, our result is reasonable.

Name ________ ____________________	Group Number: _______   Section Number:________

Spiritual Safety:
As an engineer, you will frequently be asked to optimize a system, and try to achieve a higher level of system efficiency. In the spiritual sense of this objective, Elder Michael A. Dunn teaches,
“I invite you to examine your life and see what’s stagnated or slowed you on the covenant pathway. Then look broader. Seek modest but makeable fixes in your life that might result in the sweet joy of being just a little better” (“One Percent Better”, Michael Dunn, October 2021 General Conference).
Write a sentence or two below describing a specific action that you might consistently do or are currently doing to help draw you closer to God.
I’m trying to attend the temple once every two weeks to figure out how to make that a more meaningful part of my relationship with God.
Physical Safety:
Remember to note the safety issues with operating the Pump Cart that you previously determined. In addition, it is important to note the following principles that will prevent damage to the pump motor and control circuitry: 
	Water flowing through the pump acts as a coolant. Therefore, you should not operate the pump at zero flowrate for more than around 1 minute, as this could cause the motor to overheat.
	The motor is rated at 2 hp or 1500 W. If you run the motor above 100% speed, carefully monitor the power to make sure it does not exceed this amount.
	Turn off the pump before turning off the main power.
Please alert the instructor or TA if you have a safety incident. As always, long pants, closed toed shoes and safety glasses must be worn at all times.

All team members should strive to make the team function better through various roles: observer, recorder, devil’s advocate, etc. Ask for each other’s input and opinions, help each other, and try to come to consensus after an appropriate amount of brainstorming and analysis.

Background: Pumps are fundamental to chemical engineering processes. This lab helps you better understand pumps by measuring an efficiency and a pump curve for the centrifugal pump on the cart. A second important principle to learn is that valves are used to control flow rate. 
Project: You will control the pump and control valve, and collect needed data, using a web interface. Do the pre-lab, get a laboratory-provided laptop, go to the cart, and perform the indicated activities. 
	Pre-Lab Preparation: Answer the following questions to prepare for the data collection and analysis
	What is the equation to calculate a pump or compressor efficiency? 

Efficiency = actual work/theoretical maximum work

Work output/power input

	The equation to calculate shaft work delivered to the fluid in terms of readily measured flow quantities is  W ̇_s=V ̇  ΔP. Define the quantities on the right side of the equation. Which particular ΔP on the Pump Cart needs to be measured? 

V = volumetric flow rate, in other words the volume of material flowing past a certain point per second
Delta P = change in pressure between the inlet and outlet

	How does one measure electrical work delivered to the pump? Be specific about what two quantities need to be measured.

We need the electrical energy that the pump is receiving which we can find with current and voltage.



	What is pressure head? How would you calculate pressure head from readily measured flow quantities?
Pressure/density*gravity
So we could measure the pressure and density of the liquid, or we could instead set up an energy equation and set the kinetic + potential + pressure at the inlet equal to the same three properties at the outlet. Then if we put the inlet and outlet at the same height, potential would disappear and we could measure the volumetric flowrate at the inlet and outlet and say the pressure head at one side plus the velocity head (v^2/2g) equals the pressure head at the other side plus the velocity head at that side. Then we could simplify that into the change in pressure and end up with the equation in the other problem.

	Login into the laptop using one student’s CAEDM credential.

	Explore: What is the difference between manual vs. auto control? How does this affect the control valve position? Note that the actual flow rate may not match the set point.

When it’s manual it sticks to the set control valve position, while when it’s on auto it tries to match the valve position to whatever is required to maintain a liquid flowrate of 10 gl/minute.

Set the motor rotation at 100% speed and use the position of the control valve to maintain flow at the values you specify. Collect needed data at each operating point to determine pump head and pump efficiency. It is possible to use the web interface to collect the data for you, download an Excel sheet with the data, and average the data so you can get more reliable pressure readings. 	Pump Efficiency and Pump Curve: Determine how efficient this pump is and produce a pump curve. 
	Show an example calculation for how you would calculate pump efficiency and pump head from one of your operating points in Part 3 a or b. (Added hint: notice the units the interface gives for the electrical power. Your pump power must be in these same units to calculate the efficiency.)

Efficiency = work output/power input

	Create 2 plots in Excel by plotting (i) pump head (vertical axis) vs. flowrate (horizontal axis), (ii) pump efficiency (vertical axis) vs. flowrate (horizontal axis). Each plot should have two curves for the two different pump speeds. Attach a copy of your plots to your report. Each student should make their own plot with their own file. Your plot should have labeled axes (with units specified in parentheses) and a key differentiating the two data series. Each experimental curve should have distinct points and not just a smoothed line. 

 
 

	How do pump efficiencies compare to what you expected?

The pump gets more efficient with higher flowrates. I would hypothesize that that happens because the control valve is more open and so more of the pump’s power is being used for the flowrate. This makes sense and matches with what I expected.

	Comment on the shape of the pump and efficiency curves and how this information would assist an engineer making design decisions in a real operating environment. Also comment on how you could modify the pump cart in order to extend the pump curve to lower head values (and higher flow rates).

As the flowrate increases, the efficiency does too. As the pump pressure head goes down, the efficiency does as well. That means that as an engineer you could prioritize high flowrates and low pressures while operating the pump to achieve higher efficiencies and waste less energy. You could modify the pump cart by increasing it’s ability to have high flowrates, perhaps by increasing the diameter of the tubes.

285 Fundaments Lab: Vapor Pressure
Name: 	Group Number: _______   Section Number:________
Other team members: 
(Circle the name of the person who acted as leader/coordinator)
Spiritual Safety:
In this lab, you observe how temperature, pressure, and phase changes in a system depend on time and external influences, and how equilibrium can take time to establish. In our spiritual lives, we also experience changes and growth that take time. How can understanding the need for patience and steady effort in physical systems help us appreciate the Lord’s timing in helping us reach spiritual ‘equilibrium’ or steadiness in our lives? (Write a sentence or two)
We can see that sometimes we need to be patient while we wait for things to work out and that even if things seem wrong or difficult right now we can hope that eventually things will settle out (“reach equilibrium”) and improve.
Physical Safety:
While handling the syringes or flask there is the possibility of an accidental spill. You should at all times wear long pants, closed toed shoes, and safety glasses. Gloves are recommended. If a syringe is not closed properly the fluid could be expelled. If liquids are spilled they must be cleaned up promptly. Please alert the instructor or TA if you have a safety incident. 
For the last part of the lab you will be dealing with a hot plate and flask; be sure to handle with care and use appropriate caution. 
Begin your lab by holding a team planning session (5 minutes) 
1.	Review the lab and read the safety and background sections if you haven’t already.  
2.	One person should serve as leader/coordinator. All team members should strive to make the team function better through various roles: observer, recorder, devil’s advocate, etc. Ask for each other’s input and opinions, help each other, and try to come to consensus after an appropriate amount of brainstorming and analysis.
3.	Make a plan for how you will complete the lab activities. Each person should fill out their own lab report as activities are completed. At the end of the hour, after cleaning up, get the TA to initial the end of your report.
Background
As a chemical engineer you need strong intuition about how pressure is created in systems that are a pure component vs. a mixture. Vapor pressure or saturation pressure is a temperature-dependent property of a molecule that can be measured and tabulated and therefore frequently can be looked up online. One potentially confusing thing is that the tabulated vapor pressure of a molecule may not be the actual pressure of the vapor or gas phase for a particular situation, in other words, vapor pressure is not necessarily the pressure of the vapor! This lab is to help you understand the following two key cases.
•	Pure-component system: 
o	If a system contains a pure liquid (species A) and nothing else, then the pressure of the system must be above the vapor pressure of molecule A. 
o	If the system contains two phases (liquid A and vapor A) then the system pressure is exactly at the vapor pressure of A. The amount of A in the gas phase will adjust (gas will convert to liquid and vice-versa) in order to maintain that pressure. 
o	If the system contains only vapor A then the system pressure must be below the vapor pressure of A, and will be determined by an equation of state such as the ideal gas law.
•	Pure liquid plus a gas mixture: An important engineering situation is a pure liquid, species A, with a gas space above it. 
o	If the gas is a mixture of A and B then the partial pressures of the two gases sum to form the total pressure of the gas phase, or of the system. For example, you commonly encounter liquid water with a mixture of water vapor and air above it, at a total pressure equal to atmospheric pressure. The amount of water in the gas phase will adjust (gas will convert to liquid and vice-versa) in order to maintain its partial pressure at the vapor pressure for water (just like for the pure-component case above). The remainder of the gas will be air. The partial pressure of air will be given by an equation of state, such as the ideal gas law. Thus, the total pressure of the gas phase depends on, but is not the same as, the vapor pressure of water for this system.
Project
The behavior of two-phase systems will be compared to gas-only systems. This can be accomplished by using a syringe. In addition, you will heat water in a flask on a hot plate and collect data to explain the observed behavior. To determine the temperature-dependent vapor pressures for most substances you can use an online search. For water you can use an online steam table or a steam table app on your phone. You may want to start part 3 first and then take measurements as you do the other parts, as it will take the longest.
Lab 
1.	Pressure in a syringe (water and ethanol)
a.	Mathematically how is absolute pressure related to gauge pressure? Note that the atmospheric pressure in Provo is typically 0.84 atm or 85 kPa.
Mathematically, absolute pressure is the gauge pressure plus the local atmospheric pressure

b.	What are the vapor pressures of ethanol and water at 22 ̊C?
Ethanol: 6647.2 Pa, or 6.6472 kPa
Water: 2645.5 Pa, or 2.6455 kPa
c.	Put about 5 mL of ethanol in a 30 mL syringe, if not already present. Do this by pouring a few mL into a cup or beaker first and drawing the liquid into the syringe. Remove any air from the syringe. To do this, point the exit port vertically upward and carefully push the plunger up, so that any air is expelled. Close the valve on the syringe tubing to block the opening for the next step.

d.	Push and pull on the plunger of the syringe in order to change the volume inside the syringe. What do you observe in terms of phases, pressure forces, and other physical behavior? How is it different when you push vs. pull the plunger? Physically explain your observations in terms of vapor pressure and atmospheric pressure. 
Bubbles formed when I pulled the plunger and the pressure dipped down.
When the volume in the syringe is increased, the internal pressure decreases, and once the vapor pressure is greater than the internal pressure some of the ethanol evaporates until the vapor pressure is equal to the syringe pressure again.

e.	Add 15 mL of air into your syringe (along with the ethanol) and again plug the tip. Repeat your experiment above. What is different in this case and what is the same when you push vs. pull? Explain your observations. 

There were no bubbles formed this time or if there were they were much smaller and difficult to see with the visible eye
the pressure from the air inside the syringe is still higher than ethanol's vapor pressure and so it doesn’t boil. This means you don’t get lots of obvious bubbles, although the ethanol will continue evaporating until the ethanol’s partial pressure reaches its vapor pressure	

f.	Repeat your experiment in parts d and e with water instead of ethanol. Do you notice any differences between the two liquids? 
The bubbles that formed were larger and fewer before floating to the surface. It also felt harder and the “pull back recoil” was stronger

More energy was needed to evaporate water due to its lower vapor pressure. There was also less boiling due to the lower vapor pressure.

2.	Pipetting liquids (ethanol and water)
When pipetting liquids, sometimes it is observed that the liquid is “drippy” and keeps coming out of the pipette. Here you will explore this phenomenon. 
a.  Obtain 4 unused, dry disposable pipettes. Pour a few mL of ethanol in a small cup or beaker. Pour a few mL of water in another cup or beaker. 
 
b. Gently squeeze the bulb of a pipette as shown in the picture. Insert the tip of the pipette in the liquid, keeping the bulb squeezed. Then release the pressure on the bulb so that it sucks the liquid into the stem of the pipette. Do not remove the tip of the pipette from the liquid until the bulb is fully expanded. If you mess up this procedure, start over with a new dry pipette.

c. Remove the pipette from the beaker, while holding the tip downward and suspended above the beaker to catch any liquid. Make observations for the next two minutes. Repeat this for both liquids, using a new pipette each time.

Water had 0 and 3 drops
Ethanol had 17 and 21 drops

d. Explain your observations in terms of the physical principles explored in this lab.

Water has stronger intermolecular forces and a high surface tension as well as stronger capillary action. All of that means that while ethanol will drip out of the pipette more water won’t.

e. Put used pipettes in the garbage can, but keep the syringes (empty) with the lab equipment.

3.	Mixtures with temperature change (water) – For this step you will need to use the flask with water that has a pressure gauge and thermocouple. Use some insulated gloves available in the lab when handling the flask. Under no circumstances should you heat the water temperature above 70 oC or to a pressure greater than 2.5 psi. 
a.	Write down the initial temperature and pressure of the flask system. Carefully place the flask on the hot plate. Ensure that tube leading to the pressure gauge isn’t kinked and that the bottom of the flask is fully in contact with the heat plate. Plug in and turn on the heat plate to about 50% of full scale to begin heating the water in the flask. As the water heats, record several (4 or 5) measurements of temperature and pressure. Turn off the hot plate when the temperature reaches 65 oC.

c.	Submit a plot of points showing the temperature versus pressure for the heating and cooling measurements you made. Make sure the plot is properly labeled so that someone looking at it will be able to distinguish which measurements were made during heating (or cooling).
